problem: The gloss on interrupt latency ('the longest time before the OS answers a device') blurs two different things: the delay from the interrupt arriving to the OS starting the handler, and the full device response time. A student may take the second meaning.
fix: Real-time OSes use priority scheduling and a bounded interrupt latency: the time from a device interrupt arriving to the OS starting that device's handler. The worst-case (longest) value of this delay is what real-time design must bound.

problem: The caption says the bars show when each type 'dominated', but the bars overlap (time-sharing runs to 1985 while the PC bar starts at 1980), so 'dominated' contradicts what the reader sees.
fix: The bars show roughly when each type was the main way computers were used; neighbouring eras overlap, for example time-sharing and the early PC from 1980 to 1985.

problem: The short turn given to each user is called a time slice but the synonym used by many textbooks, quantum, is never given, so a student meeting 'time quantum' in a question paper may not connect it.
fix: The OS gives each user a short turn, called a time slice (also called a time quantum), then switches.
